paths.title: How ChatGPT came to be
paths.blurb: From words as numbers to a model that follows instructions.

steps.why: Words become vectors, so computers can compare meanings.
A network that reads a whole sentence and writes another one.
Attention fixes the memory bottleneck of Seq2Seq.
Drops recurrence entirely and uses attention alone.
Pre-training on unlabeled text, then fine-tuning for each task.
Scale a language model up and it learns tasks from examples in the prompt.
Learning what humans prefer from comparisons instead of hand-written rewards.
Uses human feedback to make a language model follow instructions.
A simpler way to train on human preferences, without a separate reward step.

paths.title: How computers learned to see
paths.blurb: Deeper and smarter image networks, up to transformers and text-guided vision.

steps.why: Shows that depth with small filters works well.
Gets accuracy from clever blocks instead of just more layers.
Skip connections make very deep networks trainable.
Connects every layer to all later ones to reuse features.
Scales depth, width and resolution together.
Treats an image as a sequence of patches and uses a Transformer.
Learns images and text together, so you can search images with words.

paths.title: Finding things in images
paths.blurb: Detection and segmentation, from region proposals to real-time.

steps.why: Detects objects by proposing regions and classifying them.
Detects objects in a single pass, fast enough for real time.
Labels every pixel, and works with very little training data.

paths.title: How AI creates images
paths.blurb: From compressing images to generating new ones.

steps.why: Learns a smooth latent space you can sample from.
Two networks compete: one creates fakes, one spots them.
Generates images by learning to remove noise step by step.
Runs diffusion in a compressed space, making it much cheaper.
Links text and images, which lets text guide generation.

paths.title: Training deep networks well
paths.blurb: The techniques that made deep networks stable and trainable.

steps.why: Randomly switching off neurons reduces overfitting.
Normalizing layer inputs speeds up and steadies training.
Normalization that works for sequence models and small batches.
An optimizer that adapts the step size for every parameter.
Fixes how weight decay works with Adam.
Skip connections let gradients reach early layers.

paths.title: Making language models bigger, cheaper and more useful
paths.blurb: Scaling, efficiency, tools and new architectures.

Strong open models trained on public data.

glossary.attention: A mechanism that lets a model weigh which parts of the input matter most for each output, instead of treating every part equally.
glossary.self-attention: Attention where every word in a sequence looks at every other word in the same sequence to build its representation.
glossary.multi-head attention: Running several attention operations in parallel so the model can look at different relationships at once.
glossary.transformer: A neural network built from attention layers instead of recurrence. It is the basis of modern language models.
glossary.positional encoding: Extra information added to tokens so the model knows the order of the words.
glossary.embedding: A list of numbers that represents a word, image or other item, so that similar items get similar numbers.
glossary.token: A small chunk of text (a word or part of a word) that a language model reads as one unit.
glossary.softmax: A function that turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1.
glossary.gradient descent: A way to train a model by repeatedly nudging its parameters in the direction that reduces the error.
glossary.backpropagation: The algorithm that works out how much each parameter contributed to the error, so gradient descent can update it.
glossary.loss function: A number that measures how wrong the model's predictions are. Training tries to make it small.
glossary.overfitting: When a model memorizes its training data and does poorly on new data.
glossary.regularization: Techniques that discourage a model from overfitting, such as dropout or weight decay.
glossary.dropout: A regularization trick that randomly switches off neurons during training so the network cannot rely on any single one.
glossary.weight decay: A penalty that keeps the model's weights small. It is a form of regularization.
glossary.batch normalization: Rescaling a layer's inputs for each mini-batch to keep training stable and faster.
glossary.layer normalization: Like batch normalization, but it normalizes across the features of a single example, which suits sequence models.
glossary.learning rate: How big a step the optimizer takes at each update.
glossary.optimizer: The algorithm that updates the model's parameters during training, such as SGD or Adam.
glossary.momentum: An optimizer trick that keeps moving in a consistent direction by averaging past gradients.
glossary.mini-batch: A small subset of the training data used for one update.
glossary.epoch: One full pass through the training data.
glossary.hyperparameter: A setting chosen by the person, such as the learning rate, rather than learned by the model.
glossary.parameter: A number inside the model that is learned during training.
glossary.vanishing gradient: When gradients shrink as they travel back through many layers, so the early layers barely learn.
glossary.skip connection: A shortcut that adds a layer's input to its output, which makes very deep networks easier to train.
glossary.residual connection: Another name for a skip connection: the layer only learns a correction to its input.
glossary.convolution: A small filter slid across an image to detect patterns such as edges.
glossary.CNN: Convolutional neural network, a network built mainly from convolutions and used for images.
glossary.RNN: Recurrent neural network, which reads a sequence step by step and carries a memory forward.
glossary.LSTM: A type of RNN with gates that help it remember information over longer sequences.
glossary.encoder: The part of a model that turns the input into an internal representation.
glossary.decoder: The part of a model that generates output from an internal representation.
glossary.pre-training: Training a model first on a large general dataset before adapting it to a specific task.
glossary.fine-tuning: Continuing to train a pre-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset.
glossary.transfer learning: Reusing knowledge learned on one task to help with another.
glossary.few-shot learning: Getting a model to do a new task from just a handful of examples.
glossary.zero-shot: Doing a task with no examples, only an instruction.
glossary.in-context learning: A model picks up a task from examples placed in its prompt, without any change to its weights.
glossary.language model: A model that predicts the next word (or token) from the ones before it.
glossary.masked language model: A model trained by hiding some words and asking it to predict them.
glossary.autoregressive: Generating one token at a time, each based on the tokens before it.
glossary.prompt: The text instruction or examples given to a language model.
glossary.chain of thought: Prompting a model to write out its reasoning steps before giving the answer.
glossary.hallucination: When a model states something fluent but false.
glossary.retrieval: Looking up relevant documents to give a model extra information.
glossary.perplexity: A measure of how surprised a language model is by text. Lower is better.
glossary.BLEU: A score that compares machine-translated text with human translations. Higher is better.
glossary.GLUE: A benchmark made of several language-understanding tasks.
glossary.ImageNet: A large image dataset with 1,000 categories, used as a standard benchmark for vision models.
glossary.object detection: Finding and labeling objects in an image, usually with boxes.
glossary.segmentation: Labeling every pixel of an image with a class.
glossary.generator: In a GAN, the network that creates fake samples.
glossary.discriminator: In a GAN, the network that tries to tell real samples from fake ones.
glossary.autoencoder: A network that compresses data into a small code and then reconstructs it.
glossary.latent space: A compressed internal space where a model represents data, so that nearby points mean similar things.
glossary.KL divergence: A measure of how different one probability distribution is from another.
glossary.diffusion model: A generative model that learns to create data by gradually removing noise.
glossary.contrastive learning: Learning by pulling similar examples together and pushing different ones apart.
glossary.graph neural network: A network that learns from data made of nodes and the connections between them.
glossary.reinforcement learning: Learning by trial and error, where an agent gets rewards for good actions.
glossary.policy: The rule a reinforcement-learning agent uses to choose actions.
glossary.Q-learning: A reinforcement-learning method that learns how valuable each action is in each situation.
glossary.reward model: A model trained to score outputs by how much humans would prefer them.
glossary.RLHF: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: tuning a model using human preference judgments.
glossary.scaling law: A predictable relationship between model size, data, compute and performance.
glossary.FLOPs: A count of arithmetic operations, used to measure how much compute something needs.
glossary.low-rank adaptation: Fine-tuning by training small added matrices instead of all of the model's weights.
glossary.state space model: A sequence model that carries a compact hidden state forward, so its cost grows linearly with length.
